\chapter{Morning}
\label{ch:ta-morning}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \ta{காலை} for morning and state accurately that its origin is uncertain, rather than asserting a Sanskrit source the dictionary itself only hedges at.}

Say kālai, repeat the source's own \textquotedblleft{}possibly\textquotedblright{} instead of dropping it, and read atikaalai as a transparent ati- plus kālai compound.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ta{காலை}]{\ta{காலை} (kālai) — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} an honestly uncertain etymology}

\label{lesson:TA-C26-kaalai}



\begin{quote}
Tamil's neighbours each had a confidently-sourced story for their \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} word — Sanskrit, or clearly native. Tamil's own word for morning is different: even Wiktionary itself isn't sure where it comes from.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{காலை}} (\textbf{kālai}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning}\textquotedblright{} — has an etymology that Wiktionary itself only hedges at: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{possibly} from Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{काल्य}} (\emph{kālya}).\textquotedblright{} That's a real hedge from the source itself, not one this lesson is adding for caution's sake. Complicating things further: the related word \textbf{\ta{கால்}} (\emph{kāl}) carries \textbf{six} entirely distinct etymologies in Tamil — \textquotedblleft{}leg/foot,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}irrigation channel,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}forest,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}wind,\textquotedblright{} a Sanskrit-derived \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} sense, and a conjunction meaning \textquotedblleft{}if, when\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{\ta{காலை}} may be an accusative-type form built on the \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} sense specifically, or may not be. Be honest: this is genuinely \textbf{less settled} than Kannada's confidently-native morning word or Telugu's confidently-Sanskrit one. Don't manufacture certainty the primary source itself doesn't have.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Wiktionary does confirm one solid fact: \textbf{\ta{பகல்}} (already met, Chapter 17, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{daytime}\textquotedblright{}) is listed as \ta{காலை}'s \textbf{coordinate term} — the two words sit side by side in the same semantic field, whatever \ta{காலை}'s deeper root turns out to be. And \textbf{\ta{அதிகாலை}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{early dawn}\textquotedblright{}) is confirmed, per the Tamil Lexicon, as a fully transparent compound: \textbf{ati-} (\textquotedblleft{}excessive, very\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ta{காலை}}, glossed simply as \textquotedblleft{}early dawn\textquotedblright{} by the Tamil Lexicon.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \textquotedblleft{}atikaalai\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}early dawn,\textquotedblright{} a transparent ati- + kālai compound
\end{itemize}

(\textbf{ati-} (\textquotedblleft{}very\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ta{காலை}} — a transparent compound for \textquotedblleft{}early dawn.\textquotedblright{})
